procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated in the provided text, but it can be inferred that the case originated in a trial court where Shajahan and Raja Mohammad were convicted.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 03.09.2010 of the High Court of Madras in Criminal Appeal No. 69 and 1094 of 2006 respectively.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Shajahan and Raja Mohammad filed appeals (Criminal Appeal No. 69 and 1094 of 2006) before the High Court of Madras challenging their conviction. The High Court dismissed their appeals. The State also filed an appeal for conviction under Section 396 IPC, and the High Court enhanced the sentence of imprisonment from ten years to imprisonment for life.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Shajahan and Raja Mohammad, being aggrieved by the High Court's decision, approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal Nos. 697-698 of 2012. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeals.

directions: While maintaining the conviction under Section 396 IPC, the sentence of imprisonment imposed upon the appellants-Basheer, Shajahan and Babu @ Nawab Sahib is modified as ten years of imprisonment.
Since the appellants are stated to be in custody for more than ten years, the appellants are ordered to be released forthwith, if not required in any other case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 396 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) should be set aside.

facts: Five accused committed dacoity in a pawn shop.
During the dacoity, one person who was sleeping inside the shop was murdered; one accused (A4) sat on his chest and strangled him while another (A2) held his legs.
The trial court and the High Court both convicted the appellants under Section 396 IPC (dacoity with murder).
Stolen jewels recovered from two of the appellants were identified by the shop owner, linking them to the crime.
law: Under Section 396 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), if a murder is committed by any one person during the course of a dacoity, all individuals who are conjointly committing the dacoity are liable to be convicted for dacoity with murder.
This liability applies even to those who did not directly participate in the murder itself, beyond their participation in the dacoity.
application: The Court found that the appellants were participants in the dacoity.
Since a murder was committed by one of the dacoits during the crime, the Court applied the principle of joint liability under Section 396 IPC.
Therefore, all the appellants involved in the dacoity were held guilty of the offense of dacoity with murder, regardless of their individual role in the killing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal to set aside the conviction. It explicitly stated that it was "maintaining the conviction under Section 396 IPC" because the law holds all participants in a dacoity liable when a murder is committed by any one of them during the offense. While the Court upheld the conviction, it did modify the sentence from life imprisonment back to ten years due to mitigating factors.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence of imprisonment imposed upon the appellants requires modification.

facts: The appellants were convicted under Section 396 IPC (dacoity with murder).
The trial court sentenced them to ten years of imprisonment.
On an appeal by the State, the High Court enhanced the sentence to life imprisonment.
The accused were not armed during the commission of the offense.
At the time of the Supreme Court's decision, the appellants had already been in custody for more than ten years.
law: The offense under Section 396 IPC is to be viewed with seriousness, especially when the dacoits are armed.
application: The Court considered the specific facts and circumstances of the case to determine the appropriate sentence.
The Court noted two key mitigating factors: the "long lapse of time" since the offense in 2002 and the fact that the accused were not armed.
Based on these factors, the Court concluded that the sentence of life imprisonment was too harsh and that the ten-year sentence originally imposed by the trial court was more appropriate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court modified the sentence of imprisonment for life, which was imposed by the High Court, back to ten years of imprisonment, as was originally directed by the trial court. Since the appellants had already been in custody for more than ten years, they were ordered to be released.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 396 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) should be set aside.
appellant_arguments: The appellants, being aggrieved by their conviction, argued that it should be set aside.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) argued that the conviction should be upheld, as evidenced by their own appeal to enhance the sentence based on that conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentence of imprisonment imposed upon the appellants requires modification.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued against the enhancement of their sentence from ten years to life imprisonment, seeking a modification or reduction.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) argued that the sentence of ten years' imprisonment was insufficient and should be enhanced to life imprisonment.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction under Section 396 of the Indian Penal Code (dacoity with murder) renders a separate conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (murder) unnecessary.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court maintained the appellants' conviction under Section 396 IPC based on the principle of joint liability, where all participants in a dacoity are responsible for a murder committed by any one of them during the act. However, the court modified the sentence from life imprisonment back to ten years, reasoning that Section 396 IPC, unlike Section 302 IPC, vests the court with 'larger discretion' to impose a penalty lesser than life imprisonment.
legal_tests_applied: Principle of Joint Liability under Section 396 IPC: 'In the course of commission of dacoity, if a dacoit commits murder, all his companions who are conjointly committing dacoity, are liable to be convicted under Section 396 IPC, although they may have no participation in the murder beyond the fact of participation in the dacoity.'

Principle of Sentencing Discretion under Section 396 IPC: 'Though the offence under Section 396 IPC is to be viewed with seriousness, for the conviction under Section 396 IPC, larger discretion is vested with the court insofar as there is possibility of imposing a penalty lesser than death or imprisonment for life for the conviction under Section 396 IPC.'
why_appellant_lost: The court applied the principle of joint liability under Section 396 IPC, holding that all participants in the dacoity were liable for the murder committed during it, irrespective of their individual role in the killing.
The court determined that the prosecution's case regarding the appellants' involvement in the dacoity was not defeated even though some witnesses (PWs 21 and 22) turned hostile.
why_respondent_won: The State's position to uphold the conviction was successful because the court affirmed the legal principle that under Section 396 IPC, all individuals conjointly committing dacoity are liable for a murder committed by any member of the group during the offence.
The court found the evidence for the appellants' involvement in the dacoity to be sufficient, stating that hostile witnesses did not 'affect the prosecution case'.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning highlights a legal policy of affording judges greater sentencing flexibility for a conviction of dacoity with murder (Section 396 IPC) compared to a conviction for murder simpliciter (Section 302 IPC). This 'larger discretion' allows the court to impose a sentence less than life imprisonment, acknowledging potential differences in culpability among participants in a group crime.
